screens.title: Implementing Hooks and Off-chain Workers
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn the practical difference between runtime hooks and Off-chain Workers in Substrate, and why that distinction matters when designing pallets. Runtime hooks are deterministic functions invoked by the runtime during the block lifecycle. They must be lightweight and predictable because every validator executes them during block import. In contrast, Off-chain Workers run on node threads outside the Wasm runtime. They can make HTTP requests, perform heavier computation, and submit signed transactions back to the chain. You will see concrete examples: implementing an on_initialize hook that runs every N blocks and a basic OCW that fetches external data and prepares a signed update. We will also cover safety: how to avoid heavy logic inside hooks, how OCW-submitted data must be validated, and patterns like aggregation and signature verification to mitigate malicious submissions. By the end, you should be able to choose the right mechanism for periodic, time-sensitive tasks versus externally-sourced or resource-intensive tasks. Consider: which parts of your pallet must remain deterministic, and which can safely be moved off-chain?

screens.title: Block lifecycle and hooks
screens.narratorSegment: Let's anchor the block lifecycle. A block's processing begins with on_initialize, proceeds to execute transactions, and finishes with on_finalize. on_initialize runs before any transactions — it's the first deterministic opportunity to alter state in a block. Use it for scheduled tasks like checking expirations or incrementing counters at precise block numbers. After transactions execute, on_finalize runs and can perform summary updates or clean temporary storage based on the final state. Both hooks are executed by every validator as part of the deterministic state transition; that means any heavy computation or external input and output inside a hook will slow every validator and can threaten finality. A common example is an auction pallet: on_initialize might detect auctions that ended exactly at the previous block and prepare winners; on_finalize might emit an aggregated summary event once all transactions are applied. Misconception check: these hooks are not a replacement for background jobs — they run inside the runtime and must avoid non-determinism and long-running operations. Takeaway: place only quick, deterministic state updates in hooks and design them so their returned weight accurately reflects cost. How would you keep a hook lean if you need to process many entries?

content.html:
Module 4 › Block lifecycle
Block lifecycle and hooks
Understand deterministic timing and safe responsibilities for hooks.
Lifecycle steps
1. on_initialize(block_number) — deterministic entry point before transactions; used for scheduled checks and lightweight updates.
2. Transactions — all signed/unsigned extrinsics execute and change state.
3. on_finalize(block_number) — final state summaries, cleanup, and emitting summary events.
Common-mistake
Putting HTTP or heavy loops inside hooks. This will slow block import and must be avoided.
Example: auction check
A pallet checks for auctions that ended at or before block N. on_initialize can mark them concluded and schedule transfers. Because the logic is simple and deterministic, it belongs in a hook. If verifying external facts about the auction required network calls, that part must be moved to an OCW.
Key observations
  • Hooks run in-consensus and are executed by every validator.
  • They must return an accurate weight value for resource accounting.
  • Keep guard rails: limit loops, avoid I/O, and precompute where possible.
Key Takeaway

Treat hooks as deterministic, fast checkpoints in the block lifecycle — not as background workers.

screens.title: on_initialize — deterministic scheduler
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define on_initialize and its practical constraints. on_initialize is a Hooks trait function called at the very start of block processing and receives the current block number. Use it to run deterministic scheduled tasks that must occur before any transaction effects for that block. Typical uses include incrementing counters, expiring offers, or distributing tiny rewards. Implementation must be compact: perform index-based checks, constant-time operations, and avoid loops that scale with on-chain storage size. A good pattern is to limit processing to items due at the current block and to leave heavy aggregation or external verification to Off-chain Workers. Concrete example: increment a counter every five blocks by checking if block_number modulo five equals zero, then update storage and return a measured weight. A common misconception is to treat on_initialize as a place for long-running reconciliations — doing that risks slowing consensus. Finally, always return an accurate Weight value representing C P U and storage costs; this helps the runtime scheduler and prevents under-accounting for resources. Ask yourself: can the same change be expressed as a transaction or deferred to an OCW?

keyIdea.title: on_initialize pattern
keyIdea.text: Use it for simple, scheduled, deterministic updates with tight resource bounds and explicit weight accounting.

content.html:
Definition on_initialize
on_initialize — deterministic scheduler
A small, precise hook that runs before any transactions in a block.
Pattern
  • Accept block_number and run only cheap, deterministic checks.
  • Avoid scanning large storage; restrict work to items scheduled for this block.
  • Return a weight representing the actual resource cost.
Misconception
on_initialize is not a place for network calls or heavy computation that could vary between nodes.
Concrete example
// Example on_initialize pattern (pseudo-rust, escaped for HTML) fn on_initialize(block_number: T::BlockNumber) -> Weight { // Run every 5 blocks if (block_number % T::BlockNumber::from(5u32)).is_zero() { // Update a simple counter or expire a small batch of items // Keep operations bounded and deterministic } 0 // Return weight placeholder; replace with measured cost }
Key Takeaway

Design on_initialize for predictable, bounded updates and move heavy or external tasks out of the runtime.

screens.title: on_finalize — summaries and cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: Now focus on on_finalize. This hook runs after all transactions for the block have executed and receives the block number. Use it to perform actions that depend on the final, post-transaction state: emit summary events, clear temporary caches, or update aggregates computed across the block. Because it runs deterministically inside the runtime, the same rules apply as with on_initialize: keep it fast, bounded, and deterministic. For example, a staking pallet may compute rewards after transactions have updated stakes during the block and then write a compact summary. Misconception check: do not assume on_finalize is a safe place for validation of external data; it still executes in-consensus and must avoid input and output. If you need to reconcile external information before finalizing state, coordinate with OCWs that submit signed transactions which the on-chain logic validates. Also, ensure weights are returned where required or accounted for by runtime dispatch. Final takeaway: on_finalize is ideal when you need a deterministic snapshot-based update after all transaction effects are visible. on_finalize — summaries and cleanup means run post-transaction cleanup and deterministic summaries using final block state; keep it bounded and deterministic.. In practical terms, use cases and constraints for end-of-block logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition on_finalize
on_finalize — summaries and cleanup
Use final block state for summarizing and safe cleanup.
When to use on_finalize
  • Emit final summary events after all transactions applied.
  • Remove temporary storage entries created earlier in the block.
  • Update aggregates that require seeing the post-transaction state.
Practical hint
If the work requires heavy computation, schedule it to an OCW and accept a validated transaction later.
Concrete scenario
A ledger tracks micro-transfers during the block. After all transfers settle, on_finalize computes a compact reward snapshot and emits an event so external indexers can pick it up. Because the computation is bounded and deterministic, it’s safe in the runtime. If calculation would be expensive or require external data, delegate to an OCW instead.
Key Takeaway

Use on_finalize for deterministic final-state updates; avoid heavy computation and I/O.

screens.title: Hooks vs Off-chain Workers
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between a runtime hook and an Off-chain Worker depends on determinism, resource needs, and external dependencies. Hooks are deterministic, run in-consensus on every validator, and are ideal for time-sensitive, simple updates such as expiring entries or updating counters. OCWs run off the Wasm runtime on node threads and can perform network input and output, heavier computation, and non-deterministic actions. A clear example: use a hook to expire a time-limited order recorded on-chain. Use an OCW to fetch price feeds from an external A P I, perform aggregation, and submit the result as a signed transaction. Misconceptions arise when developers try to mix concerns: placing HTTP calls in hooks will break determinism; moving everything to an OCW without verification invites poisoned data. When using OCWs, require on-chain validation of submitted data or aggregate multiple OCW reports. Also consider node availability: OCWs run only on nodes with the std feature and suitable local keys. Practical rule-of-thumb: ask whether the operation must be executed identically by every validator using only on-chain state; if yes, it belongs in a hook. Otherwise, evaluate an OCW with appropriate verification on-chain.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: If state changes must be identical and deterministic across validators, use hooks; if you need external data or heavy processing, use OCWs with validation.

content.html:
Hooks vs Off-chain Workers
A concise comparison to decide where logic should run.
Runtime Hooks
  • Deterministic, executed by every validator.
  • Fast, bound CPU and storage work.
  • Good for scheduled state changes and cleanups.
Example
Expire an offer exactly at block X and update a counter.
Off-chain Workers
  • Run off the Wasm runtime on node threads (std feature).
  • Allow HTTP, heavy compute, and non-deterministic work.
  • Submit signed transactions back to the chain for deterministic effect.
Example
Fetch a price feed, aggregate results, and submit the median price on-chain.
Best practices
Validate OCW data on-chain.
Use aggregation or signatures to reduce trust on one node.
Keep hooks lightweight and bounded.

screens.title: Off-chain Worker basics
screens.narratorSegment: Off-chain Workers are node-local processes that run outside the deterministic Wasm runtime. They are enabled in pallets by providing AppCrypto bindings and compiling the offchain_worker function under the std feature. An OCW is invoked at block start and can check whether it's the right time to act, for example every N blocks. Within an OCW you can make HTTP requests using the runtime offchain HTTP primitives, access off-chain storage, and perform heavier computation without delaying block import. To affect on-chain state, OCWs generally prepare a call and submit it as a signed transaction using the Signer helper. This means the deterministic state change still occurs through the normal transaction validation pipeline. A key safety point: OCW results are not part of consensus until the submitted transaction is included and validated on-chain. That separation lets you do network input and output safely, but requires you to ensure that submitted results can be verified or aggregated on-chain. Practical example: an OCW fetches JSON price data, parses a numeric field, forms a Call::set_price(price, block_number), and uses Signer::any_account() to send the signed transaction. Consider the availability of local keys and how to handle missing signers.

keyIdea.title: OCW architecture
keyIdea.text: OCWs run off-runtime, fetch external data or compute, and submit signed transactions so state changes remain deterministic when applied on-chain.

content.html:
Process Flow Off-chain Worker
Off-chain Worker basics
Run non-deterministic or heavy tasks off-runtime and submit results via transactions.
OCW lifecycle
  1. Node calls offchain_worker(block_number) at block start (std feature).
  2. OCW checks timing (e.g., every N blocks) and local conditions.
  3. Perform HTTP/local compute; prepare Call and sign it using Signer.
  4. Submit signed transaction; on-chain validation applies the change deterministically.
Safety note
OCWs are not consensus actors; always validate submitted data on-chain through aggregation, signatures, or on-chain checks.
Code sketch (flow)
// offchain_worker called every block if (block_number % 5 == 0) { // send HTTP request, parse JSON // build Call::set_price(parsed_price, block_number) // let signer = Signer::::any_account(); // signer.send_signed_transaction(|_| call); }
Key Takeaway

OCWs let you gather external information and submit deterministic updates via signed transactions — but on-chain verification is essential.

screens.title: Enabling OCWs and AppCrypto
screens.narratorSegment: Before writing offchain_worker logic you must wire the OCW crypto types and key registration. This involves adding an AppCrypto implementation for your AuthorityId that maps runtime public and signature types to the expected generic types. The chapter shows using the app_crypto! macro and defining a KEY_TYPE constant for the OCW key material. This binding lets Signer find local keys to sign transactions. A concrete step is to add #cfg(feature = "std") and impl frame_system::offchain::AppCrypto for your AuthId so the runtime knows how to convert between generic and concrete signatures. Also define the crypto module and an AuthorityId alias so the Signer A P I can target the correct key type. Misconception check: this is not an on-chain permission model. The keys are local to nodes and used for signing OCW-submitted transactions. If no local key exists, Signer returns None and you should handle that gracefully—log the condition and skip submission. Finally, test the binding locally to ensure Signer::any_account() returns an account before attempting submissions. Enabling OCWs and AppCrypto means define key_type, appcrypto mappings, and ensure local authority keys exist so signer can produce signed transactions.. In practical terms, appcrypto setup, key type, and crypto glue code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Enabling OCWs and AppCrypto
Register your OCW key type and implement the AppCrypto glue.
What to add
  • Define KEY_TYPE constant for OCW keys.
  • Use app_crypto! to create concrete Public/Signature types.
  • Implement AppCrypto trait under cfg(feature = "std") for AuthId.
Runtime note
OCWs only run in the std environment. Build and run a node with std support to test them.
Example (sketch)
// KEY_TYPE and app_crypto! macro pub const KEY_TYPE: KeyTypeId = KeyTypeId(*b"ocwp"); app_crypto!(sr25519, KEY_TYPE); #[cfg(feature = "std")] impl frame_system::offchain::AppCrypto for AuthId { type RuntimeAppPublic = Public; type GenericSignature = sp_core::sr25519::Signature; type GenericPublic = sp_core::sr25519::Public; }
Handle missing signer: check Signer::any_account() and log or skip submission when None.

screens.title: offchain_worker: fetching HTTP and parsing JSON
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the core of an OCW that fetches JSON. Use sp_runtime::offchain::http::Request to make an HTTP GET and then call send() and wait() to obtain a response. Handle errors from send() and wait(), and collect the response body into a Vec before parsing. In std environments, you can use serde to deserialize JSON into a struct, or parse bytes manually. The starter code sketches fetching a price from a public A P I and converting a float into a scaled u64 for on-chain storage. Important practical checks: guard for HTTP errors, timeouts, and parsing errors; convert floats carefully (e. g., multiply by 100 for two decimals) before casting to u64 to avoid rounding surprises. screens.title: OCW safety patterns and mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: Off-chain Workers introduce a safety surface because their outputs originate off the consensus layer. The primary concern is that a malicious node could submit incorrect data. Practical mitigations include aggregation: require multiple independent OCWs to submit the same or similar values and accept a median or majority result, which reduces the power of a single attacker. If the external data provider supports cryptographic signatures, fetch signed payloads and verify signatures on-chain using known public keys. Another pattern is an unsigned transaction with a signed payload where the payload signer proves authority, but you must still check freshness and replay protection. Reputation systems can penalize bad reporters and reward accurate ones, although implementing this requires careful economic design. Finally, introduce challenge windows or time delays for critical updates so other parties can dispute suspicious submissions. Misconception check: aggregation and signatures can’t remove all risk, but they substantially raise the bar and allow you to rely on OCWs for many safe uses. The right combination depends on how critical the data is to protocol safety. OCW safety patterns and mitigations means aggregate reports, verify signatures, use challenge periods and reputation systems to make ocw-sourced data trustworthy.. In practical terms, how to reduce risk from malicious or unreliable off-chain reports. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OCW safety patterns and mitigations
Strategies to validate and harden external data before it affects state.
Aggregation
Require multiple independent OCWs to report and derive a median or consensus before accepting a value on-chain.
Cryptographic proofs
Verify signed data from trusted providers or use threshold signatures so on-chain logic can validate authenticity.

Use delays or disputes to give others time to challenge bad data and track reporter reliability when relevant.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn the practical difference between runtime hooks and Off-chain Workers in Substrate, and why that distinction matters when designing pallets. Runtime hooks are deterministic functions invoked by the runtime during the block lifecycle. They must be lightweight and predictable because every validator executes them during block import. In contrast, Off-chain Workers run on node threads outside the Wasm runtime. They can make HTTP requests, perform heavier computation, and submit signed transactions back to the chain. You will see concrete examples: implementing an on_initialize hook that runs every N blocks and a basic OCW that fetches external data and prepares a signed update. We will also cover safety: how to avoid heavy logic inside hooks, how OCW-submitted data must be validated, and patterns like aggregation and signature verification to mitigate malicious submissions. By the end, you should be able to choose the right mechanism for periodic, time-sensitive tasks versus externally-sourced or resource-intensive tasks. Consider: which parts of your pallet must remain deterministic, and which can safely be moved off-chain?

These objectives guide what you will be able to do after completing this chapter. First, you will understand the purpose and types of runtime hooks in Substrate and how they fit into the block lifecycle. Second, you will implement on_initialize and on_finalize hooks to run deterministic, efficient tasks at the start and end of blocks. Third, you will learn the concept and role of Off-chain Workers, why they run off the Wasm runtime, and when to choose them. Fourth, you will implement a basic OCW that fetches an external value and prepares a signed transaction to update the chain, and you will identify when a hook is preferable to an OCW to maintain performance and consensus safety. Each objective ties a concrete implementation skill to an engineering rationale: determinism, efficiency, and safety. You will see examples and a starter price-oracle activity that practices fetching, parsing, and submitting data. Keep in mind that the goal is not only to make code run, but to choose the correct execution model so your pallet remains performant and secure.

This second objectives slide focuses on the hands-on outcome and assessment. You will implement two concrete pieces: a small on_initialize hook that increments a counter every fixed number of blocks, and a simple Off-chain Worker that performs an HTTP GET, parses JSON, and logs or prepares a signed call. The purpose of the two implementations is to illustrate the trade-offs: the hook demonstrates deterministic state changes executed in the runtime, while the OCW shows how to gather external data and pass it into the chain in a verifiable way. You will also add a freshness check in the on-chain setter to avoid overwriting newer values with stale ones. Finally, you will learn how to evaluate the safety of OCW-submitted data using multiple mitigations such as requiring multiple reports, verifying signatures, or delaying finalization. By the end, you should be able to run the starter code, observe OCW logs in the node terminal, and reason about when each approach is the correct engineering choice.

Let's anchor the block lifecycle. A block's processing begins with on_initialize, proceeds to execute transactions, and finishes with on_finalize. on_initialize runs before any transactions — it's the first deterministic opportunity to alter state in a block. Use it for scheduled tasks like checking expirations or incrementing counters at precise block numbers. After transactions execute, on_finalize runs and can perform summary updates or clean temporary storage based on the final state. Both hooks are executed by every validator as part of the deterministic state transition; that means any heavy computation or external input and output inside a hook will slow every validator and can threaten finality. A common example is an auction pallet: on_initialize might detect auctions that ended exactly at the previous block and prepare winners; on_finalize might emit an aggregated summary event once all transactions are applied. Misconception check: these hooks are not a replacement for background jobs — they run inside the runtime and must avoid non-determinism and long-running operations. Takeaway: place only quick, deterministic state updates in hooks and design them so their returned weight accurately reflects cost. How would you keep a hook lean if you need to process many entries?

Let's define on_initialize and its practical constraints. on_initialize is a Hooks trait function called at the very start of block processing and receives the current block number. Use it to run deterministic scheduled tasks that must occur before any transaction effects for that block. Typical uses include incrementing counters, expiring offers, or distributing tiny rewards. Implementation must be compact: perform index-based checks, constant-time operations, and avoid loops that scale with on-chain storage size. A good pattern is to limit processing to items due at the current block and to leave heavy aggregation or external verification to Off-chain Workers. Concrete example: increment a counter every five blocks by checking if block_number modulo five equals zero, then update storage and return a measured weight. A common misconception is to treat on_initialize as a place for long-running reconciliations — doing that risks slowing consensus. Finally, always return an accurate Weight value representing C P U and storage costs; this helps the runtime scheduler and prevents under-accounting for resources. Ask yourself: can the same change be expressed as a transaction or deferred to an OCW?

Now focus on on_finalize. This hook runs after all transactions for the block have executed and receives the block number. Use it to perform actions that depend on the final, post-transaction state: emit summary events, clear temporary caches, or update aggregates computed across the block. Because it runs deterministically inside the runtime, the same rules apply as with on_initialize: keep it fast, bounded, and deterministic. For example, a staking pallet may compute rewards after transactions have updated stakes during the block and then write a compact summary. Misconception check: do not assume on_finalize is a safe place for validation of external data; it still executes in-consensus and must avoid input and output. If you need to reconcile external information before finalizing state, coordinate with OCWs that submit signed transactions which the on-chain logic validates. Also, ensure weights are returned where required or accounted for by runtime dispatch. Final takeaway: on_finalize is ideal when you need a deterministic snapshot-based update after all transaction effects are visible. on_finalize — summaries and cleanup means run post-transaction cleanup and deterministic summaries using final block state; keep it bounded and deterministic.. In practical terms, use cases and constraints for end-of-block logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Deciding between a runtime hook and an Off-chain Worker depends on determinism, resource needs, and external dependencies. Hooks are deterministic, run in-consensus on every validator, and are ideal for time-sensitive, simple updates such as expiring entries or updating counters. OCWs run off the Wasm runtime on node threads and can perform network input and output, heavier computation, and non-deterministic actions. A clear example: use a hook to expire a time-limited order recorded on-chain. Use an OCW to fetch price feeds from an external A P I, perform aggregation, and submit the result as a signed transaction. Misconceptions arise when developers try to mix concerns: placing HTTP calls in hooks will break determinism; moving everything to an OCW without verification invites poisoned data. When using OCWs, require on-chain validation of submitted data or aggregate multiple OCW reports. Also consider node availability: OCWs run only on nodes with the std feature and suitable local keys. Practical rule-of-thumb: ask whether the operation must be executed identically by every validator using only on-chain state; if yes, it belongs in a hook. Otherwise, evaluate an OCW with appropriate verification on-chain.

Off-chain Workers are node-local processes that run outside the deterministic Wasm runtime. They are enabled in pallets by providing AppCrypto bindings and compiling the offchain_worker function under the std feature. An OCW is invoked at block start and can check whether it's the right time to act, for example every N blocks. Within an OCW you can make HTTP requests using the runtime offchain HTTP primitives, access off-chain storage, and perform heavier computation without delaying block import. To affect on-chain state, OCWs generally prepare a call and submit it as a signed transaction using the Signer helper. This means the deterministic state change still occurs through the normal transaction validation pipeline. A key safety point: OCW results are not part of consensus until the submitted transaction is included and validated on-chain. That separation lets you do network input and output safely, but requires you to ensure that submitted results can be verified or aggregated on-chain. Practical example: an OCW fetches JSON price data, parses a numeric field, forms a Call::set_price(price, block_number), and uses Signer::any_account() to send the signed transaction. Consider the availability of local keys and how to handle missing signers.

Before writing offchain_worker logic you must wire the OCW crypto types and key registration. This involves adding an AppCrypto implementation for your AuthorityId that maps runtime public and signature types to the expected generic types. The chapter shows using the app_crypto! macro and defining a KEY_TYPE constant for the OCW key material. This binding lets Signer find local keys to sign transactions. A concrete step is to add #cfg(feature = "std") and impl frame_system::offchain::AppCrypto for your AuthId so the runtime knows how to convert between generic and concrete signatures. Also define the crypto module and an AuthorityId alias so the Signer A P I can target the correct key type. Misconception check: this is not an on-chain permission model. The keys are local to nodes and used for signing OCW-submitted transactions. If no local key exists, Signer returns None and you should handle that gracefully—log the condition and skip submission. Finally, test the binding locally to ensure Signer::any_account() returns an account before attempting submissions. Enabling OCWs and AppCrypto means define key_type, appcrypto mappings, and ensure local authority keys exist so signer can produce signed transactions.. In practical terms, appcrypto setup, key type, and crypto glue code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This screen walks through the core of an OCW that fetches JSON. Use sp_runtime::offchain::http::Request to make an HTTP GET and then call send() and wait() to obtain a response. Off-chain Workers introduce a safety surface because their outputs originate off the consensus layer. The primary concern is that a malicious node could submit incorrect data. Practical mitigations include aggregation: require multiple independent OCWs to submit the same or similar values and accept a median or majority result, which reduces the power of a single attacker. If the external data provider supports cryptographic signatures, fetch signed payloads and verify signatures on-chain using known public keys. Another pattern is an unsigned transaction with a signed payload where the payload signer proves authority, but you must still check freshness and replay protection. Reputation systems can penalize bad reporters and reward accurate ones, although implementing this requires careful economic design. Finally, introduce challenge windows or time delays for critical updates so other parties can dispute suspicious submissions. Misconception check: aggregation and signatures can’t remove all risk, but they substantially raise the bar and allow you to rely on OCWs for many safe uses. The right combination depends on how critical the data is to protocol safety. Let's summarize the key concepts you should retain. Runtime Hooks are deterministic functions executed at block lifecycle points such as on_initialize and on_finalize; they must be fast, bounded, and return a weight. Weight measures the computational resources used and helps the runtime schedule execution. Off-chain Workers run on node threads outside the Wasm runtime, enabling HTTP requests, heavy computation, and non-deterministic operations. They submit results back to the chain via signed transactions. The offchain HTTP primitive and Signer helper are central to OCW implementations. Finally, protect your chain by validating OCW-submitted data with aggregation, cryptographic proofs, challenge windows, or reputation systems. Keep these concepts in mind when designing pallets: place only deterministic work in hooks and use OCWs for expensive or external interactions with proper verification.
